examples.text: Upon my glorious ISP homepage is a wonderful piece of wisdumb […]
examples.ref: 2008, Allan A. Zarbock, The Emperor is Naked, page 58:

examples.text: Virgin Media, one of the UK's largest ISPs, has agreed to forward British music industry nastygrams to subscribers suspected of illegal file-swapping. […] But left undiscussed is the core question of why Virgin is whoring itself out like this; the law doesn't require it, and passing on letters from the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) won't make an ISP more dosh. Or will it?
examples.ref: 2008 June 16, Nate Anderson, “Cash, not idealism, behind ISP embrace of music biz”, in Ars Technica, archived from the original on 28 May 2022, retrieved 10 Feb 2009:

examples.text: Status code 451 can be used by a website such as Facebook or Twitter, or by network intermediaries like a firewall or ISP. […] Take, for example, the U.K. government’s decision in 2012 to force ISPs to block torrent site The Pirate Bay. Instead of throwing up a 403 Forbidden code, ISPs could instead return 451 to make it clear why their customers can’t see specific content.
examples.ref: 2015 December 21, Ian Paul, “Error 451 is the new Ray Bradbury-inspired HTTP code for online censorship”, in PCWorld, archived from the original on 28 Aug 2025:
